issues.legal_issue: A government may require hospitals holding public land allotted for charitable or public purposes at concessional or below-market rates to provide free treatment to economically weaker patients, even if the allotment letter or lease does not expressly state that requirement.
material_facts: The hospitals held government land under arrangements made for hospital, charitable, public-welfare, or related institutional purposes.

Some land was allotted under a policy that treated hospitals as charitable institutions and contemplated public benefit without a profit motive; other land was allotted at predetermined rates below market rates under rules requiring public institutions to serve public interests and be non-profit-making.
The allotment documents did not uniformly contain an express free-treatment condition.
The government directed the hospitals to provide free treatment to specified proportions of outpatient and inpatient patients from economically weaker sections.
issues.conclusion: The government could require the hospitals to provide free treatment, and the absence of an express condition in an allotment letter or lease did not release them from that obligation.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2 of the Charitable Endowments Act, 1890 includes relief of the poor and medical relief within charitable purposes. Rules 5 and 20 of the Delhi Development Authority (Disposal of Developed Nazul Land) Rules, 1981 permit allotment at predetermined rates and require qualifying public institutions to serve the public interest and be non-profit-making. The grant policy and applicable rules form the foundation of an allotment, which a lease may supplement but not supplant. The Court also relied on the medical-profession obligations reflected in sections 20A and 33(m) of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 and the Medical Council of India’s ethics regulations, and on the constitutional duties concerning life and health under Articles 21 and 47 and the duty in Article 51A(h). It discussed P.C. Raja Ratnam Institution v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi and Municipal Corporation of Delhi v. Children Book Trust on charitable purpose, and State of Punjab v. Mohinder Singh Chawla, Balram Prasad v. Kunal Saha, Occupational Health and Safety Association v. Union of India, Pt. Parmanand Katara v. Union of India, and Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity v. State of West Bengal on the right to health and medical duties.

rule.if: challenge_to_free_treatment_direction and hospital_uses_government_land and (charitable_public_purpose_grant or below_market_public_allotment)

predicates.challenge_to_free_treatment_direction: A hospital challenges a government direction requiring it to provide free treatment to patients in need.
predicates.hospital_uses_government_land: A hospital operates on land held under an allotment from the government.
predicates.charitable_public_purpose_grant: The land was allotted for a charitable or public-welfare purpose, including hospital services, on terms requiring public benefit or operation without a profit motive.
predicates.below_market_public_allotment: The land was allotted at a predetermined or concessional rate below its market value.

issues.definition: When a hospital challenges a free-treatment direction while using government land granted for a charitable public purpose or at a below-market rate, the government may require it to provide free treatment.

issues.legal_issue: A free-treatment obligation attached to a hospital’s use of government land for public benefit does not constitute a restriction on carrying on a profession or business that must be imposed by a statute.
material_facts: The hospitals carried on medical activities on government land allotted for public or charitable purposes, including at concessional or predetermined rates.
The free-treatment direction gave a concrete form to obligations arising from the purpose and terms of the land grants and from the medical profession’s duties to patients in need.
The hospitals argued that the direction restricted their right to carry on a profession or business and therefore required statutory enactment.
issues.conclusion: The free-treatment obligation was not a restriction under Article 19(6) on the right protected by Article 19(1)(g), and a new statute was not required to issue the directions.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(g) and 19(6) protect the right to carry on a profession, trade, or business and govern restrictions on that right. The Court held that the direction did not impose a new restriction: it gave practical effect to obligations inherent in the public-purpose land grant and the medical profession. Under Article 162, the executive may act in a field in which the legislature has power to legislate, absent a constitutional or statutory bar. The Court relied on Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab and Indian Drugs & Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Punjab Drugs Manufacturers Association on executive policy-making, and distinguished Kharak Singh v. State of U.P., Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala, and State of M.P. v. Thakur Bharat Singh, which concerned executive action infringing fundamental rights without lawful authority.

predicates.challenge_to_free_treatment_direction: A hospital challenges a government direction requiring it to provide free treatment to patients in need.
predicates.hospital_carries_on_medical_services_on_: A hospital provides medical services while holding land allotted by the government for a public or charitable purpose.
predicates.free_treatment_is_inherent_in_public_pur: The public-purpose grant and the hospital’s professional obligations already entail service to patients who cannot afford treatment.

issues.definition: If a hospital challenges a free-treatment direction while providing medical services on public land and the obligation is inherent in the public-purpose grant, the direction is not treated as a restriction on carrying on the profession.

issues.legal_issue: Requiring compliance with a free-treatment obligation is not a unilateral alteration of a hospital’s lease or the imposition of a new contractual liability when the obligation arises from the policy and rules governing the original land grant.
material_facts: A committee reviewed the hospitals’ existing free-treatment facilities, conducted inquiries, heard hospitals including one of the affected hospitals, and made recommendations that the government accepted.
The hospitals were required to show cause and filed replies before the directions were issued.

The applicable grant policy and, for certain allotments, the governing rules already provided for public-purpose or non-profit obligations; some allotment documents also reserved authority to alter terms and conditions.
issues.conclusion: The direction was not a unilateral imposition of a new obligation or a unilateral novation of the lease; it gave enforceable form to obligations already arising from the grants and governing policy or rules.
issues.legal_principle: A contract cannot ordinarily be novated unilaterally, but the Court held that this was not a case of imposing a fresh liability beyond the original grant. The policy and rules governing the allotments supplied the relevant obligations, and the committee process included inquiry and an opportunity for hospitals to be heard. The Court distinguished Delhi Development Authority v. Joint Action Committee, Allottee of SFS Flats, which concerned a fresh liability outside the original contractual terms.

predicates.challenge_to_free_treatment_direction: A hospital challenges a government direction requiring it to provide free treatment to patients in need.
predicates.grant_policy_or_rules_impose_public_purp: The policy or rules governing the original land grant require the institution to serve a public purpose or operate without a profit motive.
predicates.hospitals_were_consulted_before_directio: A committee investigated the relevant practices, heard affected hospitals, and the hospitals had an opportunity to respond before the direction was issued.

issues.definition: When the grant policy or rules already impose public-purpose obligations and affected hospitals were consulted before a direction gave those obligations practical form, the direction is not a unilateral new contractual obligation.

issues.legal_issue: A ruling requiring similarly situated hospitals to provide free treatment applies to hospitals that were not parties to the earlier proceeding when that ruling was affirmed by a reasoned Supreme Court order.
material_facts: An earlier public-interest proceeding addressed free treatment obligations for hospitals that had received government land, including hospitals treated as similarly situated.
The earlier ruling was affirmed when the Supreme Court dismissed special leave petitions by a reasoned order specifying the free-treatment obligation.
The hospitals in the present appeals contended that the earlier ruling did not apply to them because they had not been parties to that proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The earlier ruling applied to similarly situated hospitals whether or not they had been parties to that proceeding; the Court also examined the present hospitals’ claims on their merits.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the reasoned Supreme Court order affirming the earlier public-interest ruling as binding precedent for similarly situated institutions. It concluded that the earlier ruling was not confined to the hospitals formally joined in the proceeding. The Court additionally considered the current appeals afresh on their merits.

predicates.challenge_to_free_treatment_direction: A hospital challenges a government direction requiring it to provide free treatment to patients in need.
predicates.hospital_is_similarly_situated_to_hospit: The hospital has the relevant characteristics of the hospitals covered by an earlier public-interest ruling on free treatment.
predicates.prior_ruling_was_affirmed_by_reasoned_su: The Supreme Court affirmed the earlier ruling by a reasoned order.

issues.definition: When a hospital challenges a free-treatment direction, is similarly situated to hospitals covered by an earlier public-interest ruling, and that ruling was affirmed by a reasoned Supreme Court order, the earlier ruling applies to it.
